The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), let $M$ carry an orientation in the
sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]] (so that its
charts that are oriented in that orientation have orientation-preserving
transition maps), and let $\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection. This item
fixes the metric volume form, the flux of a current through oriented $3$-faces
and finite-chain charges. The orientation of $M$ is an independent datum: it is
not determined by the metric and not by the time orientation.

**(a) Metric volume density and volume form.** Let $(U,x)$ be an oriented
chart, with metric components $g_{ab}=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (a)). Define the **metric volume
density**

$$w:=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}>0\qquad\text{on }U,$$

a strictly positive smooth function because $g_{ab}$ is smooth and
$g_p$ is nondegenerate. In the chart define the local $4$-form

$$\mathrm{vol}_{g,U}:=w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3,$$

with the exterior product of [[def-wedge-product-of-differential-forms]] and the
coordinate covector fields of
[[prop-local-coordinate-expression-for-a-differential-form]]. That these local
forms agree on chart overlaps and therefore define one smooth nowhere-vanishing
$4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ on $M$ — the **metric volume form** — is proved in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (a), together
with the reading statement of clause (b) there: in every oriented chart
$\mathrm{vol}_g=w\,dx^0\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^3$, and on every positively
oriented $g_p$-orthonormal basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $T_pM$ one has
$\mathrm{vol}_{g,p}(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=1$.

**(b) Current flux through oriented $3$-faces and chains.** Let $J$ be a
smooth vector field on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **current
$3$-form** of $J$ is the contraction

$$\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g,$$

the interior product of the $4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ with $J$
([[def-interior-product-of-a-form-by-a-vector-field]]).

By a **smooth singular $k$-simplex** of $M$ — the convention of the library
definition `def-smooth-singular-simplex` (differential-geometry track),
restated here so this page is self-contained — we mean a map
$\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ whose domain is the standard $k$-simplex
$$\Delta^k=\Bigl\{t\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:t_i\ge0,\ \textstyle\sum_it_i=1\Bigr\},$$
for which there exist an open set $O\subseteq A^k=\{t\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:\sum_it_i=1\}$
containing $\Delta^k$ and a smooth map $\bar\sigma:O\to M$ with
$\bar\sigma|_{\Delta^k}=\sigma$; the extension is not part of the simplex
data, and degenerate parametrizations are allowed. With the integration of
forms over such simplices
([[def-integral-of-a-form-over-a-smooth-singular-simplex]]), a **$3$-face** is
a smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$, and the **flux of $J$ through
$\sigma$** is the real number

$$\Phi_J(\sigma):=\int_\sigma\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

A **finite smooth singular $k$-chain** — the convention of the library
definition `def-smooth-singular-chain-and-cochain-complexes`, restated here —
is a finite formal real linear combination $\Sigma=\sum_i c_i\sigma_i$ of
smooth singular $k$-simplices. For such a $3$-chain the **flux of $J$ through
$\Sigma$** is defined additively,

$$\Phi_J(\Sigma):=\sum_i c_i\,\Phi_J(\sigma_i),$$

a definition independent of the written expression for $\Sigma$, because a
finite formal sum is evaluated by adding the finitely many coefficients and
inserting a zero coefficient changes nothing. $\Phi_J(\Sigma)$ is the **charge**
of the current $J$ assigned to $\Sigma$ when the model reads $J$ as a conserved
current; that reading belongs to the physical postulates and is not part of
this definition.

**(c) Non-null faces and their unit normals.** A $3$-dimensional linear subspace
$H\subseteq T_pM$ is **nondegenerate** for $g_p$ when the restriction of $g_p$
to $H$ is nondegenerate, equivalently when $H\cap H^\perp=\{0\}$ in the
orthogonality of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. A
smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$ is **non-null at** a parameter point $t$
when the span of the three velocity vectors
$\sigma_*\partial_1|_t,\sigma_*\partial_2|_t,\sigma_*\partial_3|_t$ has
dimension $3$ and is nondegenerate at $\sigma(t)$, and **non-null** when this holds at every
parameter point. For a non-null face the **unit normal** $\nu$ at that point is
the unique vector of $T_{\sigma(t)}M$ with $\nu\in H^\perp$,
$g(\nu,\nu)\in\{-1,+1\}$ and $(\nu,\sigma_*\partial_1,\sigma_*\partial_2,
\sigma_*\partial_3)$ a positively oriented basis of $T_{\sigma(t)}M$; its
existence, uniqueness and its sign $\varepsilon:=g(\nu,\nu)$ are proved in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (c), together
with the density identity of clause (c) used to read $\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$ on
such a face. Rank-deficient faces and rank-three faces with degenerate induced
metric are not assigned a unit normal; their flux is defined
by the $3$-form $\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$ itself, as in clause (b).

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, so that $TM$ carries its canonical smooth
structure. Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. A **smooth vector field** on $M$ is a
smooth section

$$ X:M\to TM $$

of the tangent-bundle projection $\pi:TM\to M$. Thus $\pi\circ X=\operatorname{id}_M$.

Equivalently, for each $p\in M$ the value $X(p)$ is a tangent vector in $T_pM$,
and the dependence on $p$ is smooth with respect to the canonical smooth
structure on $TM$.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be an oriented, time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, with metric-selected Levi-Civita connection $\nabla$. Let $\mathcal U\subseteq M$ be open, let $u,V,s\in C^\infty(\mathcal U,\mathbb R)$, and let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $\mathcal U$. Define
$$\Box_g u:=\nabla^a\nabla_a u,\qquad |du|_g^2:=g^{ab}(\nabla_a u)(\nabla_b u).$$
If $\Box_g u=Vu+s$, define the symmetric covariant tensor
$$T_{ab}[u,V]:=(\nabla_a u)(\nabla_b u)-\frac12g_{ab}\bigl(|du|_g^2+Vu^2\bigr),$$
the vector current $J_X^a:=g^{ac}T_{cb}X^b$, and the scalar deformation term $K_X:=T_{ab}\nabla^{(a}X^{b)}$, where $\nabla^{(a}X^{b)}=(\nabla^aX^b+\nabla^bX^a)/2$.

For a finite smooth singular $3$-chain $\Sigma=\sum_{i=1}^k c_i\sigma_i$ with $k\ge0$ and $c_i\in\mathbb R$, take each simplex $\sigma_i$ to be a map $\Delta^3\to\mathcal U$ that extends smoothly to a map into $M$ on an open neighborhood of $\Delta^3$ in its affine span. Here
$$\Delta^3:=\{(t_0,t_1,t_2,t_3)\in\mathbb R^4:t_j\ge0,\ \sum_{j=0}^3t_j=1\},$$
with its standard orientation from the ordered vertices $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$, where each $e_j$ is the $j$th standard basis vector of $\mathbb R^4$. Define the local flux by
$$\Phi_{J_X}(\Sigma):=\sum_{i=1}^k c_i\int_{\Delta^3}\sigma_i^*(\iota_{J_X}\mathrm{vol}_g).$$

Here $\mathrm{vol}_g$ is the oriented metric $4$-form whose expression in an oriented chart is $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and $\iota_{J_X}\mathrm{vol}_g$ is the $3$-form that sends $(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3)\in(T_pM)^3$ to $\mathrm{vol}_{g,p}(J_X(p),Y_1,Y_2,Y_3)$ at each $p\in\mathcal U$. The map $\sigma_i^*$ is pullback of differential forms, and each simplex integral uses the pullback form-integration convention of the metric-volume current-flux definition listed in the following references section. Linearity makes the sum independent of the written chain representation. The integral uses the differential-form convention on null faces and assigns no flux to a chain with points outside $\mathcal U$; it never extends $J_X$ outside $\mathcal U$. In length coordinates, if $u$ has unit $[u]$, then $V$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-2}$, $s$ has unit $[u]\mathrm m^{-2}$, and the components of $T$ have unit $[u]^2\mathrm m^{-2}$; no physical normalization of $u$ or $X$ is imposed.

space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $n$ be an observer at $p$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]). Write $h:=h_n$,
$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,n)=0\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) and
$\mathbb Rn=\{\lambda n:\lambda\in\mathbb R\}$. Then:

1. $h:T_pM\to T_pM$ is linear, $h(n)=0$, $h(v)=v$ for every $v\in n^{\perp}$
   and $h\circ h=h$; its kernel is $\ker h=\mathbb Rn$, its image is
   $\operatorname{im}h=n^{\perp}$, and
   $T_pM=\mathbb Rn\oplus n^{\perp}$ is an orthogonal direct sum: every
   $v\in T_pM$ has the unique decomposition

   $$v=-g_p(v,n)\,n+h(v),$$

   in which $-g_p(v,n)n\in\mathbb Rn$ and $h(v)\in n^{\perp}$.
2. For all $v,w\in T_pM$ the **projection identity**

   $$g_p(h(v),h(w))=g_p(v,w)+g_p(v,n)g_p(n,w)$$

   holds; in particular $g_p(h(v),h(v))=g_p(v,v)+g_p(v,n)^2$.
3. $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive
   definite.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector
$n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$. Because
$g_p(n,n)=-1\neq0$, an observer is timelike and in particular nonzero
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Observers at $p$ exist:
the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and
$n:=N_p/\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}$ satisfies $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and
$g_p(n,N_p)=-\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}<0$, where the square root is the
nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]; then $-n$ is a unit timelike
vector with $g_p(-n,N_p)>0$, so it is not an observer, and the two vectors
$n,-n$ point in opposite time directions.

**(b) Rest space.** For an observer $n$ at $p$, the **rest space** of $n$ is
the $g_p$-orthogonal complement of the line $\mathbb Rn$,

$$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM: g_p(v,n)=0\},$$

in the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. It is
a linear subspace of $T_pM$. The further facts that $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and
that the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite are proved
in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]; they are consequences, not
part of the definition.

**(c) Spatial projection.** The **spatial projection** of the observer $n$ is
the map

$$h_n:T_pM\longrightarrow T_pM,\qquad h_n(v):=v+g_p(n,v)\,n .$$

The map is linear because $g_p$ is bilinear, its image is contained in
$n^{\perp}$, and it fixes $n^{\perp}$ pointwise; that it is the
$g_p$-orthogonal projection onto $n^{\perp}$ with kernel $\mathbb Rn$ is
proved in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]].

**(d) Scope.** An observer at $p$ is a single tangent vector. It is not an
ordered basis or frame of $T_pM$, not a chart, not a field of observers such as
the congruences defined later on this page, and not a curve or a worldline: no
parametrized curve, clock reading, proper time or measurement is attached to
$n$ by this definition. The physical reading of an observer as the direction
of an ideal clock's worldline, and the measurement interpretation of the
observer-relative quantities introduced later on this page, belong to the
physical postulates and unit conventions of the framework and are not asserted
here.

$$\Box_g u:=\nabla^a\nabla_a u,\qquad |du|_g^2:=g^{ab}(\nabla_a u)(\nabla_b u).$$
If $\Box_g u=Vu+s$, define the symmetric covariant tensor
$$T_{ab}[u,V]:=(\nabla_a u)(\nabla_b u)-\frac12g_{ab}\bigl(|du|_g^2+Vu^2\bigr),$$
the vector current $J_X^a:=g^{ac}T_{cb}X^b$, and the scalar deformation term $K_X:=T_{ab}\nabla^{(a}X^{b)}$, where $\nabla^{(a}X^{b)}=(\nabla^aX^b+\nabla^bX^a)/2$.

For a finite smooth singular $3$-chain $\Sigma=\sum_{i=1}^k c_i\sigma_i$ with $k\ge0$ and $c_i\in\mathbb R$, take each simplex $\sigma_i$ to be a map $\Delta^3\to\mathcal U$ that extends smoothly to a map into $M$ on an open neighborhood of $\Delta^3$ in its affine span. Here
$$\Delta^3:=\{(t_0,t_1,t_2,t_3)\in\mathbb R^4:t_j\ge0,\ \sum_{j=0}^3t_j=1\},$$
with its standard orientation from the ordered vertices $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$, where each $e_j$ is the $j$th standard basis vector of $\mathbb R^4$. Define the local flux by
$$\Phi_{J_X}(\Sigma):=\sum_{i=1}^k c_i\int_{\Delta^3}\sigma_i^*(\iota_{J_X}\mathrm{vol}_g).$$

Here $\mathrm{vol}_g$ is the oriented metric $4$-form whose expression in an oriented chart is $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and $\iota_{J_X}\mathrm{vol}_g$ is the $3$-form that sends $(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3)\in(T_pM)^3$ to $\mathrm{vol}_{g,p}(J_X(p),Y_1,Y_2,Y_3)$ at each $p\in\mathcal U$. The map $\sigma_i^*$ is pullback of differential forms, and each simplex integral uses the pullback form-integration convention of the metric-volume current-flux definition listed in the following references section. Linearity makes the sum independent of the written chain representation. The integral uses the differential-form convention on null faces and assigns no flux to a chain with points outside $\mathcal U$; it never extends $J_X$ outside $\mathcal U$. Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector
$n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$. Because
$g_p(n,n)=-1\neq0$, an observer is timelike and in particular nonzero
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Observers at $p$ exist:
the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and
$n:=N_p/\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}$ satisfies $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and
$g_p(n,N_p)=-\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}<0$, where the square root is the
nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]; then $-n$ is a unit timelike
vector with $g_p(-n,N_p)>0$, so it is not an observer, and the two vectors
$n,-n$ point in opposite time directions.

**(b) Rest space.** For an observer $n$ at $p$, the **rest space** of $n$ is
the $g_p$-orthogonal complement of the line $\mathbb Rn$,

$$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM: g_p(v,n)=0\},$$

in the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. It is
a linear subspace of $T_pM$. The further facts that $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and
that the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite are proved
in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]; they are consequences, not
part of the definition.

**(c) Spatial projection.** The **spatial projection** of the observer $n$ is
the map

$$h_n:T_pM\longrightarrow T_pM,\qquad h_n(v):=v+g_p(n,v)\,n .$$

The map is linear because $g_p$ is bilinear, its image is contained in
$n^{\perp}$, and it fixes $n^{\perp}$ pointwise; that it is the
$g_p$-orthogonal projection onto $n^{\perp}$ with kernel $\mathbb Rn$ is
proved in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]].

**(d) Scope.** An observer at $p$ is a single tangent vector. It is not an
ordered basis or frame of $T_pM$, not a chart, not a field of observers such as
the congruences defined later on this page, and not a curve or a worldline: no
parametrized curve, clock reading, proper time or measurement is attached to
$n$ by this definition. The physical reading of an observer as the direction
of an ideal clock's worldline, and the measurement interpretation of the
observer-relative quantities introduced later on this page, belong to the
physical postulates and unit conventions of the framework and are not asserted
here.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim:
For each component multiply $U_{i,tt}-U_{i,xx}+\sum_jV_{ij}U_j=S_i$ by $U_{i,t}$ and sum over $i$. The product rule gives
$$\partial_t\frac12|U_t|^2-\partial_x(U_t\cdot U_x)+\partial_t\frac12|U_x|^2+U_t^{\mathsf T}VU=U_t\cdot S.$$
Because $V$ is symmetric and independent of $t$, $U_t^{\mathsf T}VU=\partial_t(\tfrac12U^{\mathsf T}VU)$. Thus with $e:=\tfrac12(|U_t|^2+|U_x|^2+U^{\mathsf T}VU)$ the identity is $\partial_te-\partial_x(U_t\cdot U_x)=U_t\cdot S$.

Integrate step 1.1 over $[-R,R]$. By the Schwartz assumptions, the boundary term $[U_t\cdot U_x]_{-R}^{R}$ tends to $0$ as $R\to\infty$. The derivative of the energy density is bounded locally in $t$ by an integrable multiple of $(1+|x|)^{-2}$: its terms are products of derivatives of $U$ through order two and the bounded coefficient $V$ times such products. Thus [F1] applies to the energy density and gives $E'(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}\partial_t e\,dx$. Taking the limit in the integrated identity from step 1.1 yields $E'(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}U_t\cdot S\,dx$. Positive semidefiniteness in [A1] also gives $E\ge\tfrac12\|U_t\|_2^2\ge0$.

By [F2] and step 2.1, $E'\le\|U_t\|_2\|S\|_2\le\sqrt{2E}\|S\|_2$. For $\varepsilon>0$, differentiation yields
$$\frac{d}{dt}\sqrt{E+\varepsilon}=\frac{E'}{2\sqrt{E+\varepsilon}}\le\frac{\|S\|_2}{\sqrt2}\sqrt{\frac{E}{E+\varepsilon}}\le\frac{\|S\|_2}{\sqrt2}.$$
Integrate from $0$ to $t$ and let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ to obtain the claimed estimate, including times at which $E=0$.

Let $N\ge1$, $I:=[0,T)$ with $0<T\le\infty$, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $I$. Let $U,S\in C^\infty(J\times\mathbb R,\mathbb R^N)$. Write $\operatorname{Sym}_N(\mathbb R)$ for the real symmetric $N\times N$ matrices and use the Euclidean dot product and norm on $\mathbb R^N$. Let $V\in C^\infty(\mathbb R,\operatorname{Sym}_N(\mathbb R))$ be bounded, independent of $t$, and positive semidefinite at every $x$, meaning $z^{\mathsf T}V(x)z\ge0$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^N$. Assume $U$ and all its mixed derivatives of total order at most two, and $S$, are Schwartz in $x$ locally uniformly for $t\in J$: for every compact $K\subset J$, every such derivative $D$ and every integer $m\ge0$, $\sup_{t\in K,x\in\mathbb R}(1+|x|)^m|DU(t,x)|<\infty$, and the analogous bounds hold for $S$. If
$$U_{tt}-U_{xx}+V(x)U=S,$$
define
$$E(t):=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(|U_t|^2+|U_x|^2+U^{\mathsf T}V(x)U\bigr)\,dx,$$
where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and $\|v(t,\cdot)\|_2^2:=\int_{\mathbb R}|v(t,x)|^2\,dx$ for any vector-valued function $v$. Then $E(t)\ge0$,
$$E'(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}U_t\cdot S\,dx,\qquad\sqrt{E(t)}\le\sqrt{E(0)}+\frac1{\sqrt2}\int_0^t\|S(\tau,\cdot)\|_2\,d\tau\quad(t\in I).$$
In particular $E$ is constant when $S=0$. If $t,x$ have length units and $U$ has unit $[U]$, then $V$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-2}$, $S$ has unit $[U]\mathrm m^{-2}$, $E$ has unit $[U]^2\mathrm m^{-1}$, and both sides of the square-root estimate have unit $[U]\mathrm m^{-1/2}$. This abstract estimate supplies neither pointwise decay nor a reconstruction of coupled Einstein–Maxwell perturbations.

boundaries.evidence: Step 3.1 includes S=0, and its E+epsilon regularization also covers E=0 without division by sqrt(E).

Let $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters and put
$Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2$. Let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and require
$$f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}\ne0\qquad(r\in J).$$
On the smooth product $\mathcal M_J:=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times J_r\times S^2$,
use $S^2=\{(X,Y,Z)\in\mathbb R^3:X^2+Y^2+Z^2=1\}$ with its subspace
topology ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]). Specify the smooth
structure by the sphere atlas of [[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]],
Definition (b): for $\varepsilon=\pm1$, delete $p_\varepsilon=(0,0,\varepsilon)$
and use $\sigma_\varepsilon(X,Y,Z)=(X,Y)/(1-\varepsilon Z)$.
For $u=(u_1,u_2)$ and $h=u_1^2+u_2^2$, its inverse is
$\sigma_\varepsilon^{-1}(u)=(2u_1,2u_2,\varepsilon(h-1))/(1+h)$;
the transition is $u\mapsto u/h$ on $h>0$. These rational maps are smooth
on their domains. The product atlas consists of
$(x^0,r,p)\mapsto(x^0,r,\sigma_\varepsilon(p))$ on
$\mathbb R\times J\times(S^2\setminus\{p_\varepsilon\})$;
its transitions leave $x^0,r$ fixed and apply the displayed sphere transition.
The product is Hausdorff and second countable by the subspace topology from
$\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^3$, whose rational balls give a countable basis.
These charts specify its maximal smooth atlas, including when $J$ is empty.
The inclusion of $S^2$ into $\mathbb R^3$ is smooth with injective differential
in these parametrizations; its induced unit round metric is $\gamma_{S^2}$
([[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]).
Orient $S^2$ by its outward unit normal: for $p\in S^2$ and
$u,v\in T_pS^2$, define
$$ (\omega_{S^2})_p(u,v):=\det(p,u,v). $$
Thus $\omega_{S^2}$ is the positive area form of $\gamma_{S^2}$, and in the
polar chart $X=\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $Y=\sin\theta\sin\phi$,
$Z=\cos\theta$ it is $\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. The **dyonic RN
datum** is
$$g=-f(r)\,dx^0\otimes dx^0+f(r)^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\gamma_{S^2}, \qquad \mathcal F=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dx^0\wedge dr+q_m\omega_{S^2}.$$
Here $x^0$ and $r$ have units of metres, angles on $S^2$ are dimensionless,
and $M,q_e,q_m$ have units of metres. The metric components are dimensionless
in length coordinates; the nonzero coordinate components of $\mathcal F$ have
units inherited from their coordinate Jacobians. Use the orientation
$dx^0\wedge dr\wedge\omega_{S^2}$.

$$\Box_g u:=\nabla^a\nabla_a u,\qquad |du|_g^2:=g^{ab}(\nabla_a u)(\nabla_b u).$$
If $\Box_g u=Vu+s$, define the symmetric covariant tensor
$$T_{ab}[u,V]:=(\nabla_a u)(\nabla_b u)-\frac12g_{ab}\bigl(|du|_g^2+Vu^2\bigr),$$
the vector current $J_X^a:=g^{ac}T_{cb}X^b$, and the scalar deformation term $K_X:=T_{ab}\nabla^{(a}X^{b)}$, where $\nabla^{(a}X^{b)}=(\nabla^aX^b+\nabla^bX^a)/2$.

with its standard orientation from the ordered vertices $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$, where each $e_j$ is the $j$th standard basis vector of $\mathbb R^4$. Define the local flux by

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) and let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Call $G : I \to \mathbb{R}$ a **primitive of $f$ on
$I$** when $G$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ as a function on $I$ with
$G' = f$ there ([[def-derivative]]). Then:

1. **Existence.** Fix $c_0 \in I$. The function
   $$F : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad F(x) \;:=\; \int_{c_0}^x f$$
   is defined at every $x \in I$ ([[def-oriented-integral]],
   [[def-the-integral-function]]) and is a primitive of $f$ on $I$.
2. **Uniqueness up to a constant.** If $G_1$ and $G_2$ are primitives of $f$ on
   $I$ then there is a real $k$ with $G_1(x) = G_2(x) + k$ for every $x \in I$.
3. **Evaluation.** If $a, b \in I$ with $a < b$ and $G$ is any primitive of $f$
   on $I$, then
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

proof.** An integrable function need not have a primitive, and a function with a
primitive need not be integrable; this corollary is precisely the intersection
where both fundamental theorems apply, and both witnesses are on the companion
page.

Put $d:=\sqrt{m^2-Q^2}>0$. By [F6] the specified oriented integral defines $r_*$ with $dr_*/dr=f^{-1}$; its integrand is smooth on the exterior, so $r_*$ is smooth. Then $r_+-r_-=2d$, $r_+r_-=Q^2$, and
$$f(r)=\frac{(r-r_+)(r-r_-)}{r^2}>0\quad(r>r_+),\qquad f'(r)=\frac{2(mr-Q^2)}{r^3}.$$
Since $mr>mr_+=m^2+md>Q^2=m^2-d^2$, we have $f'(r)>0$ throughout the exterior. Also $f'(r_+)=(r_+-r_-)/r_+^2>0$, so near $r_+$ the positive function $f(r)$ is bounded above and below by positive multiples of $r-r_+$. Therefore the specified integral diverges to $-\infty$ as $r\downarrow r_+$; as $r\to\infty$, $f(r)\to1$, so it diverges to $+\infty$. Thus $r_*$ is strictly increasing and onto $\mathbb R$. Its derivative is nonzero everywhere, so [F7] gives a smooth local inverse at every point; strict increase makes these local inverses agree with the global inverse. It is therefore a smooth coordinate on the whole exterior.

In the polar chart, $\sqrt{|\det g|}=r^2\sin\theta$, $g^{tt}=-f^{-1}$, $g^{rr}=f$, and $g^{AB}=r^{-2}\gamma^{AB}$. Applying the divergence formula in [F2] to $g^{ab}\partial_b\psi$ gives
$$\Box_g\psi=-f^{-1}\partial_t^2\psi+\frac1{r^2}\partial_r(r^2f\partial_r\psi)+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}\psi.$$
Substitution of $\psi=\phi Y$ and the specified eigenvalue gives
$$-f^{-1}\phi_{tt}+\frac1{r^2}\partial_r(r^2f\phi_r)-\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^2}\phi=0.$$
This scalar coefficient vanishes because its product with $Y$ vanishes for all angles and $\int_{S^2}Y^2\,d\omega_{S^2}=1$. The regularity needed for these differentiations is [F8].

With $U_\ell=r\phi$ and $\partial_{r_*}=f\partial_r$, direct differentiation gives $r^2f\phi_r=r\,\partial_{r_*}U_\ell-fU_\ell$. Multiply the equation in step 1.2 by $fr$, then
$$\frac f r\partial_r(r^2f\phi_r)=\frac1r\partial_{r_*}(r\,\partial_{r_*}U_\ell-fU_\ell)=\partial_{r_*}^2U_\ell-\frac{ff'}rU_\ell.$$
Together with $-r\phi_{tt}=-\partial_t^2U_\ell$, and using $\partial_{r_*}f=ff'$, this yields the stated one-dimensional equation and $V_\ell=f[\ell(\ell+1)/r^2+f'/r]$. The derivatives are justified by [F8].

The factorization in step 1.1 gives $f>0$, and $f'>0$ there, so $V_\ell>0$ for every $\ell\ge0$. Let $m>0$ and $q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters, put $Q^2=q_e^2+q_m^2$, and assume $Q^2<m^2$. Define
$$r_\pm:=m\pm\sqrt{m^2-Q^2},\qquad f(r):=1-\frac{2m}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}\quad(r>0).$$
On the fixed exterior $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbb R_t\times(r_+,\infty)_r\times S^2$, use the exact dyonic Reissner–Nordström metric specified by the preceding mathematical definition with its mass parameter identified as $M=m$ and charges $q_e,q_m$, and set $t=x^0$. Define a real normalized spherical harmonic of degree $\ell\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ to mean a smooth real $Y:S^2\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$\int_{S^2}Y^2\,d\omega_{S^2}=1,\qquad \Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}Y=-\ell(\ell+1)Y,$$
where in the standard polar chart
$$\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}Y=\frac1{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta Y)+\frac1{\sin^2\theta}\partial_\phi^2Y.$$
Here $d\omega_{S^2}$ is the area measure of the unit round metric $\gamma_{S^2}$, and $f'(r)$ denotes the ordinary derivative of $f$ with respect to $r$. Since $r_+>0$, the basepoint $r_0:=2r_+$ lies in the exterior; define the tortoise coordinate by the oriented integral $r_*(r):=\int_{r_0}^{r}f(\rho)^{-1}\,d\rho$. For any such $Y$, let $\psi(t,r,\omega)=\phi(t,r)Y(\omega)$ be a smooth real solution of $\Box_g\psi=0$, and put $U_\ell(t,r_*):=r\phi(t,r)$. Then $r_*$ is a smooth coordinate from $(r_+,\infty)$ onto $\mathbb R$, and
$$\partial_t^2U_\ell-\partial_{r_*}^2U_\ell+V_\ell(r_*)U_\ell=0,\qquad V_\ell(r_*):=f(r)\left(\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^2}+\frac{f'(r)}r\right).$$
The potential is smooth, bounded, and strictly positive on $\mathbb R$. If $U_\ell$ and its derivatives satisfy the decay assumptions of the positive matrix-potential wave-energy theorem on the time interval considered, then
$$E_\ell(t):=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R}\left((\partial_tU_\ell)^2+(\partial_{r_*}U_\ell)^2+V_\ell U_\ell^2\right)\,dr_*$$
is constant there. In the original radial coordinate, its radial derivative term is $\frac12\int_{r_+}^{\infty}f(r)|\partial_rU_\ell|^2\,dr$; this energy loses control of $\partial_rU_\ell$ as $r\downarrow r_+$. It asserts no nondegenerate horizon-crossing derivative estimate, decay estimate, or coupled Einstein–Maxwell stability result. The coordinates $t,r,r_*$ and parameters $m,q_e,q_m$ have unit metres, $f$ is dimensionless, and $V_\ell$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-2}$. If $\psi,\phi$ have a common arbitrary field unit $\Phi$, then $Y$ is dimensionless, $U_\ell$ has unit $\Phi\,\mathrm m$, and $E_\ell$ has unit $\Phi^2\,\mathrm m$.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be an oriented, time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, with metric-selected Levi-Civita connection $\nabla$. Let $\mathcal U\subseteq M$ be open, let $u,V,s\in C^\infty(\mathcal U,\mathbb R)$, and let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $\mathcal U$. Define
$$\Box_g u:=\nabla^a\nabla_a u,\qquad |du|_g^2:=g^{ab}(\nabla_a u)(\nabla_b u).$$
If $\Box_g u=Vu+s$, define the symmetric covariant tensor
$$T_{ab}[u,V]:=(\nabla_a u)(\nabla_b u)-\frac12g_{ab}\bigl(|du|_g^2+Vu^2\bigr),$$
the vector current $J_X^a:=g^{ac}T_{cb}X^b$, and the scalar deformation term $K_X:=T_{ab}\nabla^{(a}X^{b)}$, where $\nabla^{(a}X^{b)}=(\nabla^aX^b+\nabla^bX^a)/2$.

For a finite smooth singular $3$-chain $\Sigma=\sum_{i=1}^k c_i\sigma_i$ with $k\ge0$ and $c_i\in\mathbb R$, take each simplex $\sigma_i$ to be a map $\Delta^3\to\mathcal U$ that extends smoothly to a map into $M$ on an open neighborhood of $\Delta^3$ in its affine span. Here
$$\Delta^3:=\{(t_0,t_1,t_2,t_3)\in\mathbb R^4:t_j\ge0,\ \sum_{j=0}^3t_j=1\},$$
with its standard orientation from the ordered vertices $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$, where each $e_j$ is the $j$th standard basis vector of $\mathbb R^4$. Define the local flux by
$$\Phi_{J_X}(\Sigma):=\sum_{i=1}^k c_i\int_{\Delta^3}\sigma_i^*(\iota_{J_X}\mathrm{vol}_g).$$

Here $\mathrm{vol}_g$ is the oriented metric $4$-form whose expression in an oriented chart is $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and $\iota_{J_X}\mathrm{vol}_g$ is the $3$-form that sends $(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3)\in(T_pM)^3$ to $\mathrm{vol}_{g,p}(J_X(p),Y_1,Y_2,Y_3)$ at each $p\in\mathcal U$. The map $\sigma_i^*$ is pullback of differential forms, and each simplex integral uses the pullback form-integration convention of the metric-volume current-flux definition listed in the following references section. Linearity makes the sum independent of the written chain representation. The integral uses the differential-form convention on null faces and assigns no flux to a chain with points outside $\mathcal U$; it never extends $J_X$ outside $\mathcal U$. In length coordinates, if $u$ has unit $[u]$, then $V$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-2}$, $s$ has unit $[u]\mathrm m^{-2}$, and the components of $T$ have unit $[u]^2\mathrm m^{-2}$; no physical normalization of $u$ or $X$ is imposed.

Let $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters and put
$Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2$. Let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and require
$$f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}\ne0\qquad(r\in J).$$
On the smooth product $\mathcal M_J:=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times J_r\times S^2$,
use $S^2=\{(X,Y,Z)\in\mathbb R^3:X^2+Y^2+Z^2=1\}$ with its subspace
topology ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]). Specify the smooth
structure by the sphere atlas of [[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]],
Definition (b): for $\varepsilon=\pm1$, delete $p_\varepsilon=(0,0,\varepsilon)$
and use $\sigma_\varepsilon(X,Y,Z)=(X,Y)/(1-\varepsilon Z)$.
For $u=(u_1,u_2)$ and $h=u_1^2+u_2^2$, its inverse is
$\sigma_\varepsilon^{-1}(u)=(2u_1,2u_2,\varepsilon(h-1))/(1+h)$;
the transition is $u\mapsto u/h$ on $h>0$. These rational maps are smooth
on their domains. The product atlas consists of
$(x^0,r,p)\mapsto(x^0,r,\sigma_\varepsilon(p))$ on
$\mathbb R\times J\times(S^2\setminus\{p_\varepsilon\})$;
its transitions leave $x^0,r$ fixed and apply the displayed sphere transition.
The product is Hausdorff and second countable by the subspace topology from
$\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^3$, whose rational balls give a countable basis.
These charts specify its maximal smooth atlas, including when $J$ is empty.
The inclusion of $S^2$ into $\mathbb R^3$ is smooth with injective differential
in these parametrizations; its induced unit round metric is $\gamma_{S^2}$
([[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]).
Orient $S^2$ by its outward unit normal: for $p\in S^2$ and
$u,v\in T_pS^2$, define
$$ (\omega_{S^2})_p(u,v):=\det(p,u,v). $$
Thus $\omega_{S^2}$ is the positive area form of $\gamma_{S^2}$, and in the
polar chart $X=\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $Y=\sin\theta\sin\phi$,
$Z=\cos\theta$ it is $\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. The **dyonic RN
datum** is
$$g=-f(r)\,dx^0\otimes dx^0+f(r)^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\gamma_{S^2}, \qquad \mathcal F=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dx^0\wedge dr+q_m\omega_{S^2}.$$
Here $x^0$ and $r$ have units of metres, angles on $S^2$ are dimensionless,
and $M,q_e,q_m$ have units of metres. The metric components are dimensionless
in length coordinates; the nonzero coordinate components of $\mathcal F$ have
units inherited from their coordinate Jacobians. Use the orientation
$dx^0\wedge dr\wedge\omega_{S^2}$.

The set $J$ may have several connected components. On $\{f>0\}$ choose the
time orientation $\partial_{x^0}$; on $\{f<0\}$ choose $\partial_r$. These
are smooth timelike fields on their respective open subsets because
$g(\partial_{x^0},\partial_{x^0})=-f<0$ when $f>0$ and
$g(\partial_r,\partial_r)=f^{-1}<0$ when $f<0$. Since $f$ has no zero on
$\mathcal M_J$, this defines a smooth time orientation on the whole product.
The sphere area form and the displayed two-form are global on $S^2$.

Let $N,S$ denote the north and south poles. On
$U_N:=S^2\setminus\{S\}$ and $U_S:=S^2\setminus\{N\}$, respectively,
local potential one-forms are
$$\mathcal A_N=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0+q_m(1-\cos\theta)\,d\phi,\qquad \mathcal A_S=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0-q_m(1+\cos\theta)\,d\phi.$$
Each displayed potential extends smoothly over its named included pole:
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $N$ and
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $S$. Direct differentiation gives
$d\mathcal A_N=d\mathcal A_S=\mathcal F$ on the respective patches. Their
overlap difference is $2q_m\,d\phi$; it is local potential data, not a global
real gauge function on the entire sphere. The definition assumes no $U(1)$
bundle or charge quantization. To verify pole smoothness, use local coordinates
$u=X,v=Y$ near each pole. There
$d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(u^2+v^2)$. Near $N$,
$1-\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1+Z)$, so
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1+Z)$ is smooth. Near $S$,
$1+\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1-Z)$, so
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1-Z)$ is smooth. The denominators are
nonzero on the respective named patches.

metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), let $(U,x)$ be a
smooth chart, and define the local **metric density** by
$w:=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}$ on $U$, using the matrix of metric components
in this chart. This definition requires no orientation or volume form. Write
$g^{ab}$ for the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]) and
$\Gamma^{a}{}_{bc}$ for the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in the chart.

**(a) Derivative of the density.** At every point of $U$,

$$\partial_a w=\tfrac12\,w\,g^{bc}\,\partial_a g_{bc}.$$

**(b) Trace of the Christoffel symbols.** At every point of $U$,

$$\Gamma^{b}{}_{ba}=w^{-1}\partial_a w .$$

**(c) Divergence formula.** For every smooth vector field $J$ on $M$, at every
point of $U$,

$$\nabla_aJ^a=\partial_aJ^a+\Gamma^{a}{}_{ab}J^b=w^{-1}\partial_a\bigl(w\,J^a\bigr),$$

where $\nabla_aJ^a=g^{ab}\nabla_bJ_a$ is the divergence of $J$ contracted with
the metric and $J^a$ are the components of $J$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).

The identity of (c) is a chart formula for a chart-independent scalar: the
right-hand side is independent of the chart, as the left-hand side is.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) and let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Call $G : I \to \mathbb{R}$ a **primitive of $f$ on
$I$** when $G$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ as a function on $I$ with
$G' = f$ there ([[def-derivative]]). Then:

1. **Existence.** Fix $c_0 \in I$. The function
   $$F : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad F(x) \;:=\; \int_{c_0}^x f$$
   is defined at every $x \in I$ ([[def-oriented-integral]],
   [[def-the-integral-function]]) and is a primitive of $f$ on $I$.
2. **Uniqueness up to a constant.** If $G_1$ and $G_2$ are primitives of $f$ on
   $I$ then there is a real $k$ with $G_1(x) = G_2(x) + k$ for every $x \in I$.
3. **Evaluation.** If $a, b \in I$ with $a < b$ and $G$ is any primitive of $f$
   on $I$, then
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**The scope is exactly the continuous case, and that is not a limitation of the

Let $a\le b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). The function $f$ is
**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $F\in AC[a,b]$, then $F'$ exists almost everywhere on $(a,b)$ and belongs to

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$
If $F\in AC[a,b]$ and $h$ is Lipschitz on $F([a,b])$, then $h\circ F\in AC[a,b]$.

differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

([[def-interval]]) and let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Call $G : I \to \mathbb{R}$ a **primitive of $f$ on
$I$** when $G$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ as a function on $I$ with
$G' = f$ there ([[def-derivative]]). Then:

1. **Existence.** Fix $c_0 \in I$. The function
   $$F : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad F(x) \;:=\; \int_{c_0}^x f$$
   is defined at every $x \in I$ ([[def-oriented-integral]],

2. **Uniqueness up to a constant.** If $G_1$ and $G_2$ are primitives of $f$ on
   $I$ then there is a real $k$ with $G_1(x) = G_2(x) + k$ for every $x \in I$.
3. **Evaluation.** If $a, b \in I$ with $a < b$ and $G$ is any primitive of $f$
   on $I$, then
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

proof.** An integrable function need not have a primitive, and a function with a
primitive need not be integrable; this corollary is precisely the intersection
where both fundamental theorems apply, and both witnesses are on the companion

For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Fix $t>0$ in the positive component of $\{s:E(s)>0\}$ containing $0$. Since $E$ is absolutely continuous on $[0,t]$, [F2]'s definition applied to a single subinterval gives continuity there; positivity on this component and compactness then give a positive minimum and a finite maximum for $E$ on $[0,t]$. The derivative of $h(x):=x^{-1/2}$ is bounded on this range by [F7]. If the range is a singleton then $h$ is constant on it; otherwise [F6] makes $h$ Lipschitz there by the mean value theorem. In either case [F5] makes $z:=h\circ E$ absolutely continuous. By [F3], $E'$ exists almost everywhere, and [F8] gives
$$z'(t)=-\frac12E(t)^{-3/2}E'(t)\ge-\frac C2(1+t)^{-1-\delta}.$$
The absolutely continuous fundamental theorem [F4] and the primitive evaluation [F9] now give
$$z(t)\ge E(0)^{-1/2}-\frac{C}{2\delta}\bigl(1-(1+t)^{-\delta}\bigr)\ge E(0)^{-1/2}-\frac{C}{2\delta}>0.$$
Taking inverse squares gives the claimed bound wherever $E(t)>0$ in that component.

If $E$ reaches $0$, the claimed inequality is immediate at that time. It cannot later become positive: otherwise some connected component $(a,b)$ of $\{t:E(t)>0\}$ has $a$ at or after a zero and $E(a)=0$, by continuity from [F2]. For any fixed $t\in(a,b)$ and $s\in(a,t)$, the same compact-interval argument as in step 1.1 makes $z$ absolutely continuous on $[s,t]$. Integrating with [F4] gives $z(t)\ge z(s)-C/(2\delta)$. As $s\downarrow a$, continuity gives $E(s)\to0$ and $z(s)\to\infty$, contradicting finite $z(t)$. Thus after a zero $E$ remains zero, and the bound holds throughout $I$.

For the comparison kernel $(1+t)^{-1}$, set
$$t_*:=\exp\!\left(\frac{2}{C\sqrt{E(0)}}\right)-1,\qquad E(t):=\left(E(0)^{-1/2}-\frac C2\log(1+t)\right)^{-2}\quad(0\le t<t_*).$$
The denominator is positive on this interval and tends to $0$ as $t\uparrow t_*$. By [F10], [F7], and [F8], differentiation gives $E'=C(1+t)^{-1}E^{3/2}$, so this solution is unbounded on its existence interval. Therefore the nonintegrable coefficient does not give the uniform bound proved above.

Let $a\le b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). The function $f$ is
**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.
